summary: Describes how to carry iLBC speech inside Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) packets. It also gives the details for using iLBC with MIME and the Session Description Protocol (SDP). It is an experimental specification.

eli5.summary: The codec makes pieces of voice, and this memo says how to pack them into the delivery trucks that carry live audio over the Internet.

questions: how many ilbc frames fit in an rtp packet
what is the ilbc bit rate
subtitle: How to carry compressed voice inside RTP packets.

tldr.problem: Internet Low Bit Rate Codec (iLBC) compresses speech efficiently, but RTP packets need a standard way to carry this encoded data.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines how to pack iLBC frames into RTP packets, specify the bitstream structure, and describe how to negotiate use via MIME and SDP.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now stream iLBC-compressed voice over IP networks with predictable bandwidth and latency, suitable for VoIP and videoconferencing.

today: RFC 3952 is an Experimental specification and defines the standard RTP payload format for iLBC. It is widely used in VoIP applications and remains the reference for iLBC streaming.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
iLBC (Internet Low Bit Rate Codec) is a speech compression algorithm developed by Global IP Sound (GIPS) for IP-based communications. This RFC describes how to format iLBC-compressed speech as an RTP payload so it can be sent over the Internet in real-time applications such as telephony, videoconferencing, streaming audio, and messaging.

The iLBC codec encodes speech in two possible frame lengths: 20 milliseconds at 15.2 kbit/s, or 30 milliseconds at 13.33 kbit/s. A sender may include one or more frames in each RTP packet depending on bandwidth, delay requirements, and tolerance for packet loss.
sections.eli5: iLBC is a way to shrink voice recordings. This section explains how to pack those shrunken pieces into messages sent over the Internet.

sections.title: The iLBC Codec
sections.content:
The iLBC codec compresses each audio frame (either 20 ms or 30 ms long) of 8000 Hz, 16-bit sampled speech. It uses block-independent linear-predictive coding (LPC) to achieve strong compression while maintaining quality similar to PCM with packet loss concealment, such as ITU-T G.711.

The two basic frame lengths produce fixed bit rates: a 20 ms frame generates 304 bits (15.2 kbit/s) which pack into 38 bytes, and a 30 ms frame generates 400 bits (13.33 kbit/s) which pack into 50 bytes. The codec handles lost packets gracefully by allowing degraded but understandable speech recovery.

Within each frame, bits are organized into three sensitivity classes: class 1 (most sensitive to errors), class 2 (moderately sensitive), and class 3 (least sensitive). This arrangement supports uneven level protection (ULP), a technique that protects critical bits more than less critical ones.
sections.eli5: iLBC shrinks voice to about one-tenth the normal size. It splits each voice chunk into three groups based on how much the sound matters, so the most important parts get protected better if something goes wrong.

sections.title: RTP Packet Structure
sections.content:
An iLBC-encoded RTP packet consists of an RTP header (as defined in RFC 3550) followed by one or more consecutive iLBC frames with no additional header. The RTP timestamp MUST be in units of 1/8000 of a second, reflecting the 8 kHz sampling rate.

When multiple frames are packed into a single packet, the RTP timestamp represents the oldest frame in that packet. Senders SHOULD follow these rules: do not exceed the network's maximum transmission unit (MTU), never split frames between packets, and never mix different frame modes (20 ms and 30 ms) in the same packet.

The number of frames in a packet can be determined by dividing the total octet count by the expected bytes per frame (38 for 20 ms, 50 for 30 ms). The RTP Mark bit (M bit) usage depends on the application profile (RFC 3551 recommends setting it to zero when sending frames on every frame interval without silence suppression).
sections.eli5: The message has a header that says when it was sent, then the iLBC chunks stuck together. You count the bytes to figure out how many chunks are in there.

sections.title: Bitstream Structure and Framing
sections.content:
Within each iLBC frame, bits are ordered by sensitivity class: all class 1 bits first (in table order), then class 2 bits, then class 3 bits. A 20 ms frame allocates 48 class 1 bits, 64 class 2 bits, and 192 class 3 bits. A 30 ms frame allocates 64 class 1, 96 class 2, and 240 class 3 bits.

The frame contains encoded components: line spectral frequency (LSF) parameters, a block classification code, quantized residual state samples, codebook indices and gains, and an empty frame indicator. The specific bit allocation for each component differs between 20 ms and 30 ms modes, optimizing the distribution of sensitive information across the three classes.
sections.eli5: Inside each chunk, the most important information comes first, then less important stuff. The exact order is different for 20-millisecond chunks versus 30-millisecond chunks.

sections.title: MIME and SDP Configuration
sections.content:
The iLBC payload is registered as a MIME type: audio/iLBC. Optional parameters control its use: mode (0, 20, or 30) specifies the frame length preference, ptime specifies the packet time duration as usual for RTP audio, and maxptime specifies the maximum media per packet in milliseconds.

In Session Description Protocol (SDP), the MIME type maps to RTP attributes: the encoding name is iLBC (case-insensitive) in the rtpmap attribute, and the mode parameter appears in the fmtp attribute. When both sides negotiate mode, they must use the same value; if they differ, the lower bandwidth mode (30 ms) is used by both parties. An example SDP line: a=rtpmap:97 iLBC/8000 with optional a=fmtp:97 mode=20 for 20 ms frames.
sections.eli5: Before the call, both sides swap SDP messages that say which chunk size they want to use. If one side likes 20 and the other likes 30, they use 30 (which is slower but saves bandwidth).

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
RTP packets carrying iLBC are subject to the general security considerations in RFC 3550 and applicable RTP profiles. Since the payload is encoded speech, confidentiality and authentication of the media are the primary concerns. The payload format itself has no built-in security; confidentiality is typically achieved through external encryption such as SRTP (Secure RTP).

Compression is applied end-to-end, so encryption can be applied after compression without conflict. The iLBC encoding does not exhibit significant non-uniformity in computational load across different input patterns, so it is not vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks based on pathological datagrams that cause receiver overload.
sections.eli5: If you want to keep the conversation private, use encryption on top of this format. iLBC is not an easy target for hackers trying to crash receivers.
